paras: The threatened lynching of J. N. Jones was an incident at Benton, Montana Territory, reported in March 1881, in which Jones, a man from Meagher county, narrowly escaped being lynched. He was spared on account of his family and on a promise to leave town within three days, and was said to have left the country afterward.

According to the only report found, Jones had been caught killing and skinning cattle for their hides and killing sheep dogs "to have the pleasure of seeing their owners put to great trouble." He was also accused of telling working men that their employers could not pay their wages. The report gives these charges as what "appears" to be the case, and no arrest, complaint or trial on them is mentioned.

The item says only that Jones "narrowly escaped lynching at Benton recently," without giving a date, describing who threatened him, or saying whether a crowd gathered. He was "only spared on his family's account and a promise to leave town in three days."

By the time of the report, Jones had "probably left the country," and the item warned that it would be "unhealthy for him if he returns." No report of any official action against Jones or against those who threatened him appears in the coverage.

The incident appeared in The Dillon Tribune of March 26, 1881, in "Montana Condensed," a column of items gathered from other territorial papers, where it ran under a heading printed "Merald," apparently a Herald. The note opened "We learn that" and repeated the accusations against Jones without naming their source. It took the side of those who had driven him out, ending with the warning "Look out for him." The report gives no race for Jones and uses no racial language, and no other paper's account was found.
